newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strauss-Kahn would be a realist at French fin min.
newsitem.headline: Strauss-Kahn would be a realist at French fin min.

text.p: Tipped as a likely finance minister if the left wins power in Sunday's French parliamentary election runoff, Socialist Dominique Strauss-Kahn would bring a realist's eye to bear on French economic problems.

Ousted from his National Assembly seat when his party was routed in the last election in 1993, Strauss-Kahn, 48, is poised to re-enter the corridors of power in a journey emblematic of the left's own recent history.
Strauss-Kahn, a former industry and trade minister, has emerged as the key architect of Socialist economic policy, including the party's pledge to create 700,000 new jobs.

He made his name as a strong defender of French economic interests and defender of the French concept of a mixed economy that couples measured free-market reform with the defence of a strong state role in industry.
From his opposition seat in the National Assembly, he vigorously opposed the privatisation programme enacted by Jacques Chirac, now the president, when he was prime minister in 1986-88.

A close confidant of his party leader Lionel Jospin, Strauss-Kahn has also championed the Socialist line on Europe -- Yes to Europe and monetary union but with a demand for further discussions on the details of implementing a planned euro currency in 1999.
He was among the first party leaders to suggest that the criteria in the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union be interpreted politically rather than in strict mathematical terms.

He says 'No' to overly rigid application of the Maastricht terms on economic fitness for joining the euro, including cutting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, but says being flexible does not mean being lax on public finances.
"Even if it's clear that public deficits cannot be allowed to slip, there is no point in making an unjustified dogma out of three percent." he said last month.
He has also advocated a slightly "softer" euro, saying it should be used to boost job creation and economic growth.
"If the Euro is to serve a purpose, it should not be overvalued against the dollar on the one hand and it should also contribute to stimulating the economy and unemployment," he said in early May.

Industry and trade minister in the short-lived 1991-92 government of prime minister Edith Cresson, Strauss-Kahn won the respect of the corporate sector for his role as a counterweight to what industrialists saw as Cresson's policy excesses.
He was also hailed for his diplomatic finesse when he became the first official in the Cresson government to visit Tokyo shortly after she irked the Japanese by likening them to ants.

With the same portfolio in the 1992-93 Socialist government of Pierre Beregovoy, Strauss-Kahn distinguished himself as a vocal defender of French interests in negotiations over the GATT international free trade agreement.
Married to star television journalist Anne Sinclair, Strauss-Kahn chaired the National Assembly (lower house) finance committee before joining Cresson's government in May 1991.

He was a strong advocate of the right of the state as shareholder to act as any other shareholder would, including injecting funds into firms it controls, a habit that often got France into hot water with the European Commission in Brussels.
Dominique Gaston Andre Strauss-Kahn was born on April 25, 1949 at Neuilly sur Seine, a chic western Paris suburb.

He followed in the footsteps of his lawyer father to obtain a law degree, but also studied at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes Commerciales elite business school and has advanced degrees in political science, statistics and economics.
He lectured at Nancy University in the late 1970s and worked for the national statistics office, INSEE. In 1982 he became head of the finance department of the State Planning Commission.
He entered parliament in 1986, when as a senior Socialist Party official he was elected for the Alpine Haute Savoie department. He was re-elected in 1988 for Val d'Oise near Paris.

His marriage in 1991 to Sinclair, his third wife, would probably bar him from defending government policies as a guest on her popular weekly news programme. He has four children from previous marriages. She has two children.
